problem: The chapter says a waking task is placed exactly at the tree's minimum vruntime, i.e. at cfs_rq->min_vruntime. In the kernel the value is max(old vruntime, min_vruntime − threshold), and with GENTLE_FAIR_SLEEPERS on by default the threshold is half of sched_latency. So a sleeper does get a small bounded credit (half a latency window), not exactly the minimum. The conclusion 'sleeping earns no extra CPU' is still right, but the sentence is stated too absolutely.
fix: Say: a waking task's vruntime is set to the tree minimum, or to its old value if that is larger; the kernel may also subtract up to half a sched_latency window as a small bounded sleep credit. Because the credit is capped, a task cannot hoard CPU by sleeping.

problem: The last clause, 'a normal task placed in the first band outranks everything', is confusing. A normal task is never given a priority in 0–99, and if it were it would outrank other normal tasks but still sit with the real-time band, not above everything.
fix: Replace with: 'Priorities 0–99 are the real-time band and 100–139 the normal band. A normal task always sits in 100–139; anything in 0–99 outranks every normal task.'

problem: A waking task is not always inserted in the active array. In the O(1) scheduler, if the woken task's priority is not better than the currently running task's, it is queued in the expired array so it cannot preempt the running task; only a higher-priority wakeup goes to the active array.
fix: State the rule: a woken task goes to the active array only if its priority beats the running task's; otherwise it is placed in the expired array to run in the next round. Waking a higher-priority task triggers preemption.

problem: '140 priority queues' is loose: the runqueue has two arrays of 140 lists each (280 lists in all), one array active and one expired, with a bitmap per array.
fix: Say 'two arrays of 140 priority queues each, with a bitmap per array' the first time the structure is described.

problem: 'one step gives roughly 25% more CPU' is direction-blind. Moving one step toward higher weight (nice 0 to nice −1) multiplies weight by 1.25, giving 25% more CPU; moving one step the other way (nice 0 to nice 1) gives 1024/820, about 20% less.
fix: Say: each single nice step toward greater weight multiplies the weight by about 1.25, so a task one step heavier gets roughly 25% more CPU than the task one step lighter, and the lighter one gets about 20% less.
